about: What must never break in the air, each case a worked example straight from its FAA source, the expected figure the source's own (never the code's). A case asks one engine rule by name with `input`; `want` is the answer, or the members of it that the source settles; `within` gives a figure's tolerance where the source reads it off a plotter or an E6B (its own rounding), and a figure not in `within` is exact. The engine (engine/facade/tests/flight_critical.rs), the iPhone (WingtipTests/FlightCriticalTests.swift) and Android (androidTest FlightCriticalEngineTest.kt) hold the engine to every case; CI's Flight-critical job runs them on every change.

cases.name: The handbook's wind triangle: TC 090, wind 045 at 40 kt, TAS 120 kt
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C ch. 16, Wind Triangle or Vector Analysis (Figures 16-21 to 16-23): "the WCA is 14 deg and the wind is from the left; therefore, subtract 14 deg from TC of 090 deg, making the TH 076 deg"; GS 88 knots

cases.name: No wind: the heading is the course and the groundspeed the true airspeed
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C ch. 16, Wind Triangle or Vector Analysis: "If there is no wind, the aircraft's ground track is the same as the heading and the GS is the same as the true airspeed"

cases.name: The handbook's leg in the nav log: 220 NM at 88 kt is 2:30 and about 20 gallons at 8 gal/hr; 5 deg east variation, east is least
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C ch. 16: "If the distance measures 220 NM, divide by the GS of 88 knots, which gives 2.5 hours, or 2:30 ... If fuel consumption is 8 gallons an hour, 8 x 2.5 or about 20 gallons is used"; variation "east is least (subtract)". On the equator so the true course is 090 the whole way.

cases.name: The handbook's fuel: 400 NM at 100 kt in still air is 4 hours, 20 gallons at 5 gal/hr
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C ch. 16, Fuel Consumption: "a flight of 400 NM at 100 knots GS takes 4 hours to complete. If an aircraft consumes 5 gallons of fuel per hour, the total fuel consumption is 20 gallons"

cases.name: Glide at a ratio of 9: 3,500 ft over the ground is 31,500 ft, 5.18 nm
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-3C ch. 3, Glides (p. 3-21): "The glide ratio of an airplane is the distance the airplane travels in relation to the altitude it loses. For example, if an airplane travels 10,000 feet forward while descending 1,000 feet, its glide ratio is 10 to 1"; the international nautical mile, 1,852 m (6,076.12 ft). 3,500 x 9 / 6,076.12 = 5.184 nm

cases.name: Oxygen at 12,500 ft MSL
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.211(a): "(1) At cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet (MSL) up to and including 14,000 feet (MSL) unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 minutes duration; (2) At cabin pressure altitudes above 14,000 feet (MSL) unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen during the entire flight time at those altitudes; and (3) At cabin pressure altitudes above 15,000 feet (MSL) unless each occupant of the aircraft is provided with supplemental oxygen." No oxygen or pressurised cabin in the profile; eastbound IFR, so a height off the odd thousands also draws 91.179(b)(1)'s caution.

reasons: Eastbound under IFR flies odd thousands, unless ATC assigns otherwise (14 CFR 91.179)

cases.name: 91.159 at exactly 3,000 ft above the surface: any altitude up to it, odd plus 500 above (090 magnetic, 500 ft ground)
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.159(a): "When operating above 3,000 feet above the surface" -- 3,500 ft MSL over 500 ft ground is 3,000 ft above it, not more, so any altitude to it (every 500 ft offered); above it, "on a magnetic course of zero degrees through 179 degrees, any odd thousand foot MSL altitude + 500 feet": 5,500. 4,000 and 4,500 are more than 3,000 ft up and not odd plus 500.

cases.name: VFR with no departure time: night is not ruled out, so the night's 45-minute reserve, and night left unknown
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.151(a): "(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or (2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes." With no time the larger is assumed; 45 min at 8 gal/h is 6 gal.

cases.name: The handbook's Sample Problem 1: pressure altitude 5,718 ft at 5,883 ft and 30.10 inHg
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C ch. 11, Sample Problem 1: "Airport Elevation 5,883 feet, OAT 70 °F, Altimeter 30.10 "Hg ... Find 30.10 under the altimeter heading ... It reads "-165." Therefore, it is necessary to subtract 165 from the airport elevation giving a pressure altitude of 5,718 feet ... The approximate density altitude in thousands of feet is 7,700 feet." Figure 11-3's table is in whole feet: within 2.

cases.name: The handbook's Sample Problem 1: density altitude about 7,700 ft at 5,718 ft pressure altitude and 70 F (21.1 C)
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C ch. 11, Sample Problem 1: "Airport Elevation 5,883 feet, OAT 70 °F, Altimeter 30.10 "Hg ... Find 30.10 under the altimeter heading ... It reads "-165." Therefore, it is necessary to subtract 165 from the airport elevation giving a pressure altitude of 5,718 feet ... The approximate density altitude in thousands of feet is 7,700 feet." Read off Figure 11-22's chart to the nearest hundred: within 100.

cases.name: Endurance: 40 gal usable at 8 gal/h is 5 hours, 4:30 after the day VFR reserve
cases.source: FAA-H-8083-25C ch. 16: fuel used is the burn times the time ("If fuel consumption is 8 gallons an hour, 8 x 2.5 or about 20 gallons is used"), so 40 / 8 = 5 h; 14 CFR 91.151(a)(1): "During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes", 4 gal at 8 gal/h.

cases.name: Lost comms, 91.185(c)(2): on each segment the highest of assigned, minimum and expected
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.185(c)(2): "At the highest of the following altitudes or flight levels for the route segment being flown: (i) The altitude or flight level assigned in the last ATC clearance received; (ii) The minimum altitude ... for IFR operations; or (iii) The altitude or flight level ATC has advised may be expected in a further clearance." V170: assigned 6,000 over its 5,000 minimum; V82, from where 8,000 was to be expected: 8,000 over its 7,000 and the 6,000 assigned.

cases.name: Lost comms, 91.185(c)(2)(ii): the minimum altitude where it is the highest
cases.source: 14 CFR 91.185(c)(2): "At the highest of the following altitudes or flight levels for the route segment being flown: (i) The altitude or flight level assigned in the last ATC clearance received; (ii) The minimum altitude ... for IFR operations; or (iii) The altitude or flight level ATC has advised may be expected in a further clearance." V82's 9,000 minimum is over the 6,000 assigned and the 8,000 expected.
